name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Tuesday 29 November 1983

clue.text: Ancient retainer makes criminal return wood to girl

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the word for criminal is read backwards

blocks.note: an old lag is a habitual criminal
a log is a piece of wood
a lass is a girl

explanation.surface: An old family servant somehow turns a crook into someone who brings firewood back to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: GAL from the reversed LAG, then LOG and LASS. A galloglass (also gallowglass) was a mercenary soldier kept by Irish and Scottish chiefs.
explanation.definitionFit: Galloglasses were armed followers maintained by Gaelic chieftains in medieval times, so an old-time retainer in the sense of a kept fighting man.

clue.text: Old Man might be a gillie?

blocks.note: first meaning: an old fellow, or the boss
second meaning: one who uses a gaff, the hook a fishing attendant lands salmon with

explanation.walkthrough: A gillie is a Scottish hunting or fishing attendant who gaffs the angler's catch, so the question mark asks us to read the answer as gaff-er.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaffer is informal for an elderly man or the boss, which is what Old Man means in either sense.

clue.text: Meadows - or grounds, say

indicators.note: say tells us to speak the word, so its sound counts and not its spelling

blocks.note: lees are the grounds or dregs left in a cask

explanation.surface: Grassy fields, otherwise known as open land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grounds' looks like land but means sediment.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is a poetic or old word for an open grassy field, so the plural is meadows.

clue.text: Master exhausted?

blocks.note: first meaning, a verb: to defeat or conquer
second meaning: overwhelmed, as by tiredness or emotion

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the second sense is a stretch: someone overcome is worn out and overpowered.
explanation.definitionFit: To overcome is to defeat or prevail over, and someone overcome is overpowered and helpless with fatigue.

clue.text: Theatre fan's associate

blocks.note: surface reading: an enthusiast for plays
setter's reading: the person linked with the fan in the title of Oscar Wilde's 1892 comedy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fan' looks like a theatregoer; it is the hand fan of Wilde's play, whose owner is the title character.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilde's play is named after a lady and her fan, so she is the person tied to the most famous fan in the theatre.

clue.text: Foreign women give reasons for making up

indicators.note: making up means composing or putting together, so the letters are assembled afresh

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Women from abroad explain why they make up after a quarrel, or why they wear cosmetics.
explanation.definitionFit: Señoras is the Spanish for ladies or married women, so they are women from abroad.

clue.text: No real judge of Shakespeare

blocks.note: surface reading: someone with poor taste in the plays
setter's reading: a Shakespeare heroine who only poses as a judge, a lawyer in disguise in The Merchant of Venice

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a jibe at a poor critic of the Bard; in fact it means a character who sits in judgment while not really being one.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merchant of Venice the heroine disguises herself as the young doctor of law Balthazar to decide Shylock's case, an impostor magistrate.

clue.text: Speaker has alternatives at heart

indicators.note: the heart is the middle, so one piece is placed right at the centre of the other

blocks.note: each alternative is joined by 'or', so two of them give that word twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A public speaker keeps several options in mind at the core of his talk.
explanation.walkthrough: AT goes between the two ORs, its own word 'at' doing double duty with 'heart'.
explanation.definitionFit: An orator is someone who makes formal public speeches, a speaker by profession.

clue.text: Could be the tiniest vessel with nothing in it -they're found in most homes

indicators.note: could be suggests something possible, a version of the phrase rather than the phrase as set out
with nothing in it says the zero sits among the other letters

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, after 'the' as a link
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Perhaps the smallest empty container you can imagine, the kind every household owns.
explanation.walkthrough: The O for nothing joins the letters of TINIEST VESSEL before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: By 1983 television receivers were in most households, so they are things found in most homes.

clue.text: Improving by midday?

blocks.note: first meaning: making better, correcting
second meaning: at noon the morning (a.m.) is ending

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful split: AM is morning, and by midday the morning is over.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend is to put right or better, so the present participle means getting better or correcting.

clue.text: Officers are not well placed in strikes

indicators.note: something placed in something else is set inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: biffs are blows, informal for strikes
to ail is to be unwell

explanation.surface: Police officers are off sick during industrial strikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strikes' looks like industrial action but means punches.
explanation.definitionFit: Bailiffs are law officers who serve writs and seize goods for a court or sheriff.

clue.text: Dramatist returned fresh load of fish

indicators.note: something returned goes back where it came from, so the word for fresh is read right to left
a load is carried inside something, so one piece holds the other within it

blocks.note: raw means fresh, uncooked
the cod is a fish

explanation.surface: A playwright came back from the market with a new catch of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Load of' reads as a cargo but signals that one word carries the other. Noël Coward wrote Private Lives and Blithe Spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Noël Coward was an English playwright, so he is an example of a dramatist.

clue.text: Thataway, as it were, might mean the opposite

blocks.note: surface reading: the cowboy cry pointing the way someone went
setter's reading: 'that way' is the reverse of 'this way', a statement turned around

explanation.walkthrough: The playful 'Thataway' is meant as the other way round from this way; the answer is a noun for the reverse of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The converse of a statement is its reverse or contrary, so the word names the opposite.

clue.text: Arranges to fill in the deed itself?

indicators.note: fill in describes letters lying inside the following words, filling the space within them

blocks.note: found running across the end of 'deed' and the start of 'itself'

explanation.surface: Sorts out the paperwork to complete the legal document itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fill in' and 'deed' suggest completing a legal form, but the phrase points inside the words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Edits means prepares or orders material, as an editor arranges text or film.

clue.text: Get less stupid batting to his breaks?

indicators.note: a thing that breaks falls into pieces, which are put back in a new order

blocks.note: dim means slow-witted
a batsman in cricket is in
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dull batsman is asked whether he wises up during his breaks between innings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get less stupid' reads as one idea, but 'Get less' is the definition and 'stupid' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: To diminish is to become smaller or reduce, the intransitive sense of getting less.

clue.text: Musical instrument - new model, and an odd one

indicators.note: a new version is made over, so these letters take a fresh order
odd means strange, so the letters come out in an unusual order

blocks.note: the first set of letters to rearrange
the second set of letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A music shop has a newly designed instrument and also a peculiar one.
explanation.definitionFit: A melodeon is a small reed organ or button accordion, a type of musical instrument.

clue.text: Harsh red tints need altering

indicators.note: if the letters need altering they must be changed round into another arrangement

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A painter is told that the garish red shades need toning down.
explanation.definitionFit: Strident means loud and grating, a near synonym of harsh, used of sounds or colours.

clue.text: Carter goes out on the eastern balcony

indicators.note: going out suggests things knocked about, so the letters leave their order

blocks.note: the main letters to rearrange
E is the abbreviation for eastern

explanation.surface: Someone named Carter steps out onto the east-facing balcony.
explanation.walkthrough: Carter looks like a surname, perhaps President Carter, but it is just letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A terrace can be a raised open platform or balcony in front of a building.

clue.text: Galsworthy wrote it, that's the contention

blocks.note: first meaning: John Galsworthy's 1909 play about an industrial dispute
second meaning: conflict and bitter disagreement

explanation.walkthrough: 'Contention' could read as an argument being put forward; here it means discord.
explanation.definitionFit: Strife is conflict or discord, the quarrelling sense of contention, and it is also the title of Galsworthy's play.

clue.text: Divide the pears . roughly and brew the tea

indicators.note: done roughly means handled carelessly, so the letters of the fruit end up jumbled
brewing stirs things together, so the drink's letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: the first set of letters to rearrange
the second set of letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Kitchen instructions: cut up the pears roughly and make a pot of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: To separate is to split something into parts, a direct synonym for divide.

clue.text: A sort of tailless leopard - word of honour!

indicators.note: having no tail means the final letter of the animal is cut off
a sort of suggests a version of the word, its letters sorted into a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a leopard missing its tail, sworn to on one's honour.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the D, then rearrange LEOPAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Parole originally meant a prisoner's promise not to escape, given on his honour; it comes from French for word.

clue.text: American actor reads lines and nothing more

blocks.note: BR is British Rail, whose railway lines are a crossword staple
taken as written
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A film star merely recites his script without any acting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reads lines' looks like an actor at work, but 'reads' is only a link and 'lines' means railway lines.
explanation.definitionFit: Marlon Brando was a celebrated American film actor, star of On the Waterfront and The Godfather.

clue.text: Shakespeare character is a docile type? That's about right

indicators.note: a type is a variety, so the letters come out in a different arrangement
about means around, so the shuffled letters wrap round the next piece

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a certain Shakespearean figure is meek, and is told that's roughly correct.
explanation.walkthrough: CODELIA from the letters of A DOCILE, wrapped round R.
explanation.definitionFit: Cordelia is King Lear's youngest and most loyal daughter, a character in Shakespeare's tragedy.

clue.text: Striker might be Jack?

blocks.note: first meaning: a heavy stick or golf ..., something you hit with
second meaning: a card suit, of which a jack can be one

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the jack being only one card in the suit, the jack of clubs.
explanation.definitionFit: A club is a cudgel or golf stick used for hitting, and also one of the four suits of playing cards.

clue.text: Bloomer made by form filler, perhaps - alarming thing

blocks.note: a hare's resting hollow is called its form, so the hare is what fills one
an alarm bell rings a warning

explanation.surface: Someone filling in an official form makes a blunder that causes real alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' looks like a mistake and 'form filler' like a clerk; here a bloomer is a flowering plant and the form is a hare's lair.
explanation.definitionFit: The harebell is a wild flower with blue bell-shaped blooms, so a plant that blooms.

clue.text: Songs written in the first person, say?

indicators.note: say asks us to speak the phrase out, using its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: the one in front of everyone else is the leader

explanation.surface: A comment on lyrics composed from an 'I' point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' suggests grammar, but it means whoever comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Lieder are German art songs, such as those by Schubert, set for voice and piano.

clue.text: Just Nora Lee's mistake about the sailor

indicators.note: a mistake gets things wrong, so the woman's name is written out in the wrong order
about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters go round the seaman

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, the possessive S included
AB is an able seaman

explanation.surface: A woman called Nora Lee only made an error concerning a seaman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Just' looks like 'only' but is the definition. The apostrophe S of Nora Lee's belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Reasonable means fair and sensible, matching just in the sense of fair-minded.
